18615.trajectory_category: Iterative technical scope and commercial alignment
18615.trajectory_explanation: The visible trajectory is an extended fit-and-alignment process: the offer was resized after a reported budget mismatch; marking, product, packaging, and cap requirements evolved; laboratory and legal review added dependencies; and the customer later challenged delivery time and requested extensive technical detail. The buyer eventually reported the contract signed and requested the invoice, but the last call still records payment as awaited (e1-e2, e3-e11, e14-e22). This describes the documented path, not a claim about final deal outcome or a single causal factor.

primary_evidence.paraphrase: Date-only manager worklog (time inferred): says the customer found the calculated price too high and requested a revised offer for 1,000 units/hour. This is a manager claim.
Date-only manager worklog (time inferred): says the customer was awaiting Chinese offers, lacked space for the machine, and did not expect to buy before July/August. This is a manager claim.
Customer says QR labeling will remain manual and asks whether a dry topping doser can be added; the seller says they will check with engineering and notes this is outside their usual equipment.

Customer insists on a July 17 factory visit and asks for written answers about marking integration; seller says engineering declined the dry-topping equipment, and the customer agrees to drop that option for now.

Date-only manager worklog (time inferred): reports that viscosity and density information was with a laboratory and the customer was also sending the draft contract to a lawyer. This is a manager claim.
Date-only manager worklog (time inferred): reports a container change because the label dimensions did not fit and that more time was needed to agree on the container. This is a manager claim.
Date-only manager worklog (time inferred): says a 7.5% price increase effective Aug 17 was communicated while the container choice remained unresolved. This is a manager claim.
Date-only manager worklog (time inferred): reports the customer returned to a screw cap and sent final container/cap dimensions for a corrected offer. This is a manager claim.

Customer directly says the 75-working-day production lead time is too long and proposes either reducing the advance to 50% or shortening delivery to about three calendar months; seller says they will consult the director and production.
Customer asks for a dimensioned line-layout drawing to accompany the contract.
Customer says their 65 mm container does not fit the discussed arrangement.
Customer adds that QR-code marking equipment is needed.
Customer asks whether the equipment can handle caps up to 90 mm when the current stated range is up to 80 mm.
Customer lists contract/specification questions about staffing, a missing 100 L intermediate tank and transfer pump, air-pressure reducers, cap-hopper capacity, and container-size range.
Customer asks how the dosing machine would be adjusted if product density or dose volume changes.
Customer asks how to document density and viscosity ranges for product variants; the seller offers to consult production and provide ranges for the contract.
Customer asks to include a viscosity range as well.
Customer requests a production-line video for the marking-system integrator, explaining that this could avoid waiting three months for the new line.
Customer email says a signed contract is being sent back and requests the seller's stamp/signature before electronic signing and payment.
Customer says the contract was signed on Friday.
Customer asks for the invoice by email.

manager_strong_actions: A manager worklog reports reworking the offer for lower throughput after the price concern (e1).
The seller discussed the dry-addition request with engineering, communicated that the equipment could not be supplied, and coordinated a factory visit and written integration questions (e3-e4).
Manager worklogs report revised quotations as packaging changed; the email thread later says a production-line video was sent to help the customer's marking-system integrator (e9, e19).
manager_weak_actions: No clear individual manager error is established. However, the customer was still asking for important line-layout, tank, pump, pressure, hopper, and container-range clarifications during contract review, showing that technical alignment remained incomplete at that checkpoint (e11).
The customer raised a specific delivery-time/advance-payment trade-off and the seller said they would consult internally; the cited record does not establish the resolution of that request (e10).
customer_positive_signals: The customer initiated a factory visit and requested written answers for the marking-system integration (e4).
The customer sent packaging information, requested detailed drawings and technical clarifications, and engaged in contract revisions (e9, e11, e15).
The customer pursued signature and invoicing: a signed-contract email is in the view, followed by a direct message confirming signature and a request for the invoice (e20-e22).
customer_negative_signals: Manager worklogs report early price sensitivity, comparison with Chinese suppliers, and a delayed purchase because the customer lacked space (e1-e2).
Container, label, cap, QR, and product-property requirements continued to change or need clarification during the technical and contract process (e3, e7-e18).
The customer directly objected to the 75-working-day delivery estimate and proposed alternative delivery or advance-payment terms (e10).
uncertainties: Date-only manager worklogs use inferred times and are manager claims, not contemporaneous customer speech (e0-e2, e5-e9).
The final approved machine configuration and the exact resolution of the delivery-time/advance-payment request are not established by the cited events (e10-e18).
The customer reports a signed contract, but this view does not establish whether the electronic-signing process completed or whether payment was received by Aug 31 (e20-e22).

Some technical, laboratory, financing, and legal status is available only through manager worklogs; the customer's direct messages corroborate several questions but not every reported internal milestone (e5-e9).

18773.trajectory_explanation: The buyer directly described a price/technical comparison with another supplier and a funding certificate that had to arrive before the purchase could move forward. Those dependencies extended the decision period while the seller updated the package configuration. In September the discussion advanced into document and payment arrangements, while an additional 0.33 L fit question remained technically open. This explains the visible path only and does not assign a final outcome (evidence indices 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 19).

primary_evidence.paraphrase: Buyer says another supplier was asked to quote the same task and that price and technical aspects would both be compared.
Buyer is still waiting for a competing offer and asks how semi-automatic packaging works; the seller explains the packaging alternatives.
Buyer says the competitor still has not sent its offer but he is considering the seller's equipment and expects to decide the following week.
Buyer says a funding-related certificate ordered through MFC takes six to seven working days and that a clear decision should follow once it arrives and funds are available.
Buyer says the certificate is still being checked by a lawyer and hopes funds will be available the following week; the competitor still has not replied.
Buyer reviews the listed equipment and asks clarifying questions about what the date coder marks and which parts are included.
Seller sends a revised offer removing the date coder and showing automatic and semi-automatic packaging options.
Seller and buyer discuss that the proposed no-VAT route would require cash payment; buyer asks whether a bank-card transfer is possible.
Seller proposes an IP-to-IP payment with standard paperwork and equipment described as used; buyer says he expects no problem with that arrangement.
Buyer says 0.5 L glass is a real format and 0.33 L is only a possible future order; seller says a drawing or measured photo is needed to verify the smaller format.

manager_strong_actions: The manager updated the proposal as the scope changed, offered automatic and semi-automatic packaging comparisons, and sent supporting line videos (evidence indices 4, 5, 10, 11, 15).

The manager maintained agreed check-ins while the buyer waited on financing and a competitor, then clarified the buyer's requested documents and revised the commercial paperwork (evidence indices 6, 7, 8, 9, 12, 13, 14, 17).
When the buyer asked about 0.33 L, the manager checked with production and requested bottle drawings or measured photos before confirming fit (evidence index 19).
manager_weak_actions: The equipment/packaging configuration and payment-document approach underwent several late revisions. A base configuration with separately priced options and an earlier checklist of required payment documents could have reduced repeated proposal changes (evidence indices 5, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14).

The view does not show a completed technical confirmation for the possible 0.33 L package before the payment-status message; the buyer had described it as a possible future format, so it should remain an open fit question (evidence indices 18, 19, 20).
customer_positive_signals: The buyer actively compared the offer on price and technical fit, stayed in contact while waiting for the competing supplier, and said a decision would be made even if that offer did not arrive (evidence indices 3, 7).

The buyer discussed a funding timeline, reviewed revised packaging options, provided company details for paperwork, and raised a specific additional bottle-format question (evidence indices 8, 10, 15, 16, 18, 19).
customer_negative_signals: The buyer repeatedly deferred proposal review and decision timing while a production incident, funding certificate, and competitor comparison were pending (evidence indices 2, 6, 7, 8, 9).

The project scope remained fluid: packaging options changed, the date coder was removed, and an additional 0.33 L format was raised late without a bottle drawing or dimensions (evidence indices 5, 10, 11, 18, 19).
uncertainties: Initial capacity, size, and price details are recorded in a date-only manager worklog; direct evidence confirms the multi-format project but does not independently verify every initial metric (evidence indices 0, 1).

The external funding certificate and competitor offer were not yet available during the August review; the view does not establish how either would have changed the decision (evidence indices 3, 7, 8, 9).
The 0.33 L format remained unverified without dimensions or a drawing, while the buyer described it as a possible future need (evidence indices 18, 19).

A deal-channel message says payment was received, but its sender direction is unknown and no bank document is present in the view. A separate internal comment is timestamped 28 Jul while containing later dated notes, so it was not used as customer-confirmed payment evidence (evidence indices 20, 22).

18733.trajectory_explanation: The visible path lengthened as optional conical containers changed the price and technical scope, specifications/questionnaire details were completed, and the buyer's management and legal reviewers controlled approval and contract timing. The customer later directly confirmed purchase approval and reported payment, so the preceding delay is best explained by scope and internal process rather than a visible loss of interest. This describes the trajectory only and does not assign a final outcome label (evidence indices 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12, 14, 15).

primary_evidence.paraphrase: Buyer says leadership was occupied/on leave and the equipment discussion had not yet been reached amid other priorities.
Buyer requests the final quote before contract and invoice because the higher price needs internal approval.
Buyer says the questionnaire remains incomplete because label dimensions were not recorded and he had not had time to finish it.
Buyer says the contract was forwarded to the lawyer and describes a legal review process that could take time.
Buyer says management is reconsidering the conical-container configuration because of added operating and logistics complexity.
Buyer confirms that the conical option is excluded, asks for a recalculated quote and contract, and says the active configuration has three cylindrical package positions.
Buyer directly says the purchase is approved and contract edits are being handled.
Buyer says documents are sent for signature and payment, with another responsible person still needing to process them.
Buyer does not know whether payment will happen that day or the following week and says he will check with the director.
Customer email states that payment went through. This is customer-reported payment status, not an independent bank-credit confirmation.

manager_strong_actions: The manager obtained package information, involved production in feasibility checks, and revised the proposal as the buyer considered the conical option and later removed it (evidence indices 0, 4, 7, 8).
The manager provided contract and technical follow-up, including a direct response to the buyer's concern about applying a label to the cylindrical cardboard cup (evidence indices 6, 10, 11).
manager_weak_actions: Questionnaire handling created avoidable friction: the buyer said the attachment was missing and later explained that the form was incomplete because dimensions were not recorded; the contract path depended on completing those details (evidence indices 5, 6).

Scope and price needed several revisions as the optional conical format was introduced and then removed. This was partly customer-led, but consolidating a clear base configuration plus priced options could have reduced rework (evidence indices 4, 7, 8).
customer_positive_signals: The buyer forwarded the proposal for management review, requested a revised final quote when scope changed, and provided company and package information (evidence indices 2, 4, 5).
The buyer worked through legal review and technical questions, then directly stated that the purchase was approved and later sent a signed contract (evidence indices 6, 9, 10, 13).
customer_negative_signals: The buyer could not consistently prioritize the questionnaire and equipment discussion while other work and management reviews were pending; this limited speed of specification and approval, but does not by itself show disinterest (evidence indices 3, 5, 6).
The conical-container option was reconsidered and removed after it raised additional cost and operational questions, requiring another proposal and contract adjustment (evidence indices 4, 7, 8).
uncertainties: Two date-only manager worklogs conflict on initial price acceptance; the buyer-sourced call only establishes that the proposal was forwarded for internal review (evidence indices 0, 1, 2).

The detailed starting capacity and size range are in a manager worklog; later customer calls support the cylindrical/conical scope changes but do not independently verify every initial specification (evidence indices 0, 7, 8).

Payment is self-reported by the customer, followed by a seller production handoff; there is no independent bank confirmation in the view. This is a strong indirect outcome cue and is not used to predict or assign WON/LOST (evidence indices 14, 15, 16).

18745.trajectory_explanation: The visible trajectory advanced technically and contractually, while director/investor availability and subsequent legal/accounting steps delayed the decision and payment schedule. The manager's contract omissions created avoidable rework, and repeated payment reminders irritated the buyer after the buyer said finance controlled timing. These factors describe process friction and delay; the uncertain internal 80% payment note is not used as customer-confirmed status or as an outcome label (evidence indices 2, 3, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 15, 17).

primary_evidence.paraphrase: Buyer says the price is acceptable to him and that he forwarded the proposal to the director/investor, who had not yet reviewed it.
Buyer says the director and investor are expected to decide during the week.
Buyer says the decision is nearly made, requests the complete package including commissioning, confirms the quoted price range, and notes that internal bureaucracy may delay review.
Buyer flags that the contract names the wrong director and lacks the commissioning contract, asking for both documents together.
Buyer says the director has not yet responded and the company is still waiting, although the equipment is needed.
Buyer says the director is not answering and he has no decision update.
Buyer reports director approval and says contract review will still take time, with a later check-in planned.
Buyer says payment is planned for the following Tuesday.
Buyer says the equipment is approved and awaiting payment, but says repeated daily payment questions are irritating and that accounting controls the payment day.
Internal comment stamped 24 Jul contains dated running notes through 27 Aug and a manager claim of 80% payment received; chronology is uncertain and the claim is not treated as customer-confirmed.

manager_strong_actions: The manager requested package dimensions, sent the proposal and video, checked technical fit against the containers, and continued through proposal and contract revision (evidence indices 1, 6, 7, 8).
After the buyer flagged contract defects, the manager sent a changed contract the next day and later coordinated the invoice and payment follow-up (evidence indices 7, 8, 13, 16).
manager_weak_actions: The first contract package used the wrong director title and omitted the separate commissioning agreement; the buyer had to point out both issues and ask for a complete package (evidence index 7).

Repeated payment checks were too frequent for the buyer and caused explicit irritation; aligning directly with accounting or agreeing one payment check-in could have reduced friction (evidence indices 15, 16).
customer_positive_signals: The buyer said the quoted price was acceptable personally and forwarded it to management; later he provided package information and asked for a complete contract and commissioning scope (evidence indices 1, 2, 4, 5, 6).
The buyer directly said the equipment contract was approved and described payment as awaiting the company's payment process (evidence index 15).
customer_negative_signals: Director access and internal review were slow, and the buyer often could not give an approval date (evidence indices 3, 9, 10).
The buyer became irritated by repeated payment requests, saying payment timing was handled by accounting and that he could not promise a particular day (evidence index 15).
uncertainties: The detailed unit rate and initial readiness are from a date-only manager worklog; the buyer directly confirms cylindrical packages and printing but not every initial metric (evidence indices 0, 1).

The internal comment is timestamped 24 Jul but contains later dated notes, including a 27 Aug payment claim. Its exact chronology and the claimed 80% receipt are uncertain; customer-sourced 26 Aug evidence still describes payment as awaiting accounting (evidence indices 15, 17).
The later filling-module inquiry is different scope and should not be merged with the labeler trajectory (evidence index 14).

5971.trajectory_explanation: The visible trajectory moved from contract and compliance review to a signed scan, then shifted to shipment scheduling and the permitted acceptance route. The view ends with the alternative route being checked, so it does not establish that dispatch or acceptance was completed (evidence: 3-10).

Leasing sent a contract with legal comments and accepted edits for review and agreement.
Leasing sent a scan of the signed purchase contract.

customer_positive_signals: The leasing contact reported internal circulation and sent a signed contract scan (evidence: 0,5).
The customer requested shipment timing and proposed alternatives for delivery and acceptance (evidence: 6-8,10).

No outcome labels or prior audit files were consulted for this audit; same-day status beyond the visible exchanges is not established by this view.

Counsel approval was reported, but EDI receipt and the contract's signed status remained under recheck at the last retained call; this is a process state, not evidence of a final outcome (evidence: 2,4-9).

The customer asked how long the process would take, described preparing labels and tubes, and said it wanted to secure the price before a July 1 increase because internal contract approval was complex.

manager_strong_actions: Presented a shortened production lead-time estimate, discussed label placement, and agreed to revise the specification for the requested printer-marker and cartridges (evidence: 1-2).
A covering manager took the customer's status call and responded to the stated urgency (evidence: 4).
manager_weak_actions: A manager worklog reports using the announced price increase to pressure the customer to speed approval; this is self-reported and the customer only independently confirms concern about the price window (evidence: 3-4).
customer_positive_signals: The customer proactively asked to add specific equipment and consumable details to the contract specification (evidence: 2).
The customer shared legal requirements, responded to the certificate request, and reported when counsel had approved the documents (evidence: 5-7).
customer_negative_signals: The client expressed concern about lengthy internal contract approvals and uncertainty about receiving or signing the EDI documents (evidence: 3,8-9).
uncertainties: The previous preprocessing role gave me residual familiarity with raw chronology and lifecycle-boundary corrections, so this audit is label-blind but not fully chronology-blind.
The initial product and schedule detail comes from a manager worklog rather than customer statements in the retained events.
The view ends during active document-status checks; no final outcome is established.
Run A auditor previously handled source preprocessing; this deal's paired independence is limited.

18635.trajectory_explanation: The visible trajectory centers on how a keyed can would be positioned and labeled at the desired speed, and how the customer could verify performance on its own can. The seller clearly stated the automatic-orientation speed constraint and could not provide a pre-manufacture sample test; the customer therefore focused on documenting a post-manufacture test and acceptance procedure. Contract and invoice steps advanced, and the final direct call records the customer's stated intention to pay and prepare samples, but the view does not confirm payment receipt (e1-e5, e10-e18).

primary_evidence.paraphrase: Seller says automatic rotation to align the can key limits throughput to about 1,000-1,200/hour; manually pre-positioning cans could increase speed.
Customer asks whether the final throughput will remain 1,000 cans/hour.
Customer asks whether the video is an AI visualization or a real prototype and whether its own can and label can be tested.
Seller says the example is from an earlier project, no equipment is currently available for testing, and testing will take place after manufacture.
Customer asks for contract corrections to appendices and wants the acceptance act to record whether the equipment demonstration worked and any objections at the time of demonstration.
Seller confirms receipt of the customer's contract edits and says they were sent to legal for review.
Customer says there are no remaining comments on the disagreement protocol after editing an appendix.
Customer says to proceed with signing and payment quickly and confirms the contract can be sent through EDO.
Customer says contract documents arrived but were not yet reviewed; seller says the invoice was sent, and customer will check it. Payment is not confirmed.

Customer says payment is expected that day or the next, asks the seller to prepare production, and agrees to send label rolls and 50 product cans for testing. The call records expected payment, not receipt.
Customer asks whether 70% of the current 954,000 invoice is the initial payment.

manager_strong_actions: The seller stated the throughput limit early and explained the can-positioning tradeoff, then answered questions about payment, label sensing, and the questionnaire (e1-e3, e7-e8).
The seller sent example footage, disclosed that a sample test was unavailable before manufacturing, and said the detailed acceptance test would be conducted after manufacturing (e4-e5).
The seller involved legal in the buyer's contract edits, responded to the buyer's EDO invitation and invoice questions, and coordinated the requested sample materials for a test (e10-e12, e15-e18).
manager_weak_actions: The buyer's central validation need could not be met before manufacture; the seller offered post-manufacture testing, leaving the customer exposed to a wait before seeing its own can run on the equipment (e4-e5, e16). This is a solution-capability limit, not clearly an individual manager error.

The final manager worklog states that a payment order was submitted, but same-day customer-sourced messages and call discuss payment as upcoming; this difference in timing/source should not be treated as confirmed receipt (e14, e16-e18).
customer_positive_signals: The customer engaged on throughput, key alignment, label roll requirements, service, payment terms, and testing details (e1-e8).
The customer provided packaging and label measurements, completed the questionnaire, supplied contract revisions, and accepted the revised protocol (e8-e12).
The customer directly said to sign and pay quickly, then discussed sending product cans and labels for the post-manufacture test (e13, e16-e18).
customer_negative_signals: The requested 2,000 cans/hour exceeded the seller's stated automatic-orientation rate of about 1,000-1,200/hour; no measured production result appears in the view (e1-e2).
The customer could not test its own can before ordering; it requested that testing and acceptance conditions be made explicit in the contract (e4-e5, e10).
The customer needed to resolve contract edits and asked for invoice re-delivery because the original invoice could not be opened (e10-e12, e15-e17).
uncertainties: Initial price acceptance and early readiness-to-buy are date-only manager claims rather than direct customer messages in the cited events (e0).
Actual throughput and label performance on the customer's cans are not measured in this view; the planned sample run is after manufacture (e1, e4-e5, e16).

The date-only worklog says a payment order was submitted, while customer-sourced same-day events discuss paying and ask about the 70% amount; no bank receipt or completed transfer is established here (e14, e16-e18).

The final signed-contract/payment chronology is uncertain because the manager worklog uses an inferred time and summarizes multiple milestones, while the same-day customer call describes payment as upcoming (e14, e16-e18).

6885.trajectory_category: Technical qualification and contract progressed; payment confirmation remains open
6885.trajectory_explanation: The buyer's director approved the approach after technical questions were answered, and the parties moved through contract review to a signed contract and invoice. The visible remaining steps are contract-channel confirmation and payment; the final call records expected payment, not confirmed receipt. [evidence: 5, 6, 7, 9, 11, 12, 13]

Buyer said the director approved moving to a contract for an individual entrepreneur and discussed sending container samples and using EDO.
Manager sent a standard contract and disagreement protocol and explained the next review/signature step.
Buyer said the revised contract attachment was missing and asked the seller to resend it.
Seller returned the countersigned contract and sent an invoice.
Buyer said payment was being arranged and expected it promptly; no payment proof is visible here.
Customer could not yet reach the contract signer; a half-payment appeared in a payment list, and a payment order was expected. No bank receipt is confirmed.

manager_strong_actions: Obtained a production-backed solution and explained the conveyor, side supports, sensor, and optional divider. [evidence: 1, 5, 6]
Provided a revised offer, video, and structured payment terms after the director's questions. [evidence: 5, 6]
Prepared a contract for the buyer's legal review, sent it in Word when requested, and returned the seller-signed copy with an invoice. [evidence: 7, 10, 11]

The offer/contract email was not received promptly and had to be re-sent through Telegram; the customer also later could not find the contract attachment and requested a Word copy. [evidence: 2, 10]
Pickup/carrier responsibility was clarified only after legal review, leaving two delivery clauses unresolved. [evidence: 9]

Said the director was leaning toward the seller's option, then approved starting contract preparation. [evidence: 3, 7]

customer_negative_signals: The director required additional assurance about spacing, sensing, print quality, and divider operation before settling the design. [evidence: 5]
The customer's legal review challenged delivery-risk clauses and requested the editable contract. [evidence: 9, 10]

No payment confirmation or equipment delivery/acceptance is present after the buyer's expected payment date. [evidence: 13]
The physical sample-test result is not shown. [evidence: 1, 5]
Independent audits differed on whether the observed process gap was a manager weakness; the listed action is a possible improvement, not a proven cause.

7191.trajectory_category: Scope phased to fit the buyer's new facility; contract progressed and payment remained pending

Technical questions about product transfer and bottle formats were addressed, and the buyer proceeded through contract review. The endpoint is signed paperwork and an invoice with payment timing still open, not a confirmed payment or production start. [evidence: 2, 4, 6, 9, 10, 12, 14]

The customer raised multiple document-processing questions and was unavailable while traveling, which delayed signature and payment follow-up. [evidence: 12, 13, 14]

6983.trajectory_explanation: The visible trajectory moved through a capacity revision, customer approval and contract signature, then slower installment payments under a buyer-reported credit burden. Connecting conveyor sections and a date coder were added after the main agreement, requiring further sizing and an amendment. The buyer's final payment and production-start request remain unconfirmed in the view. [evidence: 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13]
